summary: A Segment Routing Policy is an ordered list of segments, with one or more candidate paths. This document extends PCEP so that controllers and routers can create, report and manage SR Policy candidate paths. It updates RFC 8231.

plainLanguage.summary: A trip plan is a list of stops, and there may be several possible plans. This lets a central planner and the routers talk about those plans in a common language.

questions: what is an sr policy association
subtitle: How PCEP describes Segment Routing Policies, so controllers and routers can agree on each candidate path.

tldr.problem: PCEP could already set up Segment Routing paths, but those paths were not SR Policies. They could not be tied to candidate paths of the same policy learned from configuration or BGP, and they carried no color for steering.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a new PCEP association type, the SR Policy Association, that groups the LSPs (candidate paths) of one SR Policy and carries the policy identity and candidate path attributes in new TLVs. It also adds TLVs for computation priority, Explicit NULL label policy and Drop-Upon-Invalid.
tldr.outcome: PCEs and PCCs can now signal SR Policy candidate paths in a way that matches the SR Policy architecture. The RFC also updates RFC 8231 so that PCReq and PCRep become optional for SR Policy LSPs.

today: RFC 9862 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025. It updates RFC 8231 and has not been obsoleted. The color extension for non-SR-Policy paths is in RFC 9863.

sections.title: Why SR Policies Need More Than RFC 8664
sections.content:
RFC 9256 describes the Segment Routing (SR) Policy, which is steered traffic with one or more candidate paths. A candidate path is the unit used to signal a policy to a headend. RFC 8664 lets a stateful PCE compute and initiate SR paths over PCEP, but the paths it creates are not SR Policies as RFC 9256 defines them.

That leaves two gaps. PCEP-signaled candidate paths cannot be associated with candidate paths of the same policy that come from other sources, such as local configuration or BGP. And a policy cannot be tied to an intent through its color, which is needed for headend-based steering of BGP service routes.

This document fills the gaps by reusing the PCEP Association mechanism from RFC 8697. A PCEP Association corresponds to an SR Policy, and an LSP corresponds to a candidate path.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers already knew how to follow a list of stops, but not how to say which trip plan a list belonged to. This adds the name tag.

sections.title: Overview of the Extensions
sections.content:
An SR Policy is represented by a new association type, the SR Policy Association (SRPA). The candidate paths of one policy are the LSPs in the same SRPA. The extensions here encode a single segment list per candidate path; multiple segment lists are left to another document.

An SRPA carries three kinds of information: the SR Policy Identifier, the Candidate Path Identifier and the Candidate Path attributes. Three further items do not travel in the SRPA: computation priority, the Explicit NULL Label policy and Drop-Upon-Invalid behavior. The RFC introduces four new TLVs for them and for capability exchange.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the information goes on the name tag. A few extras, like how urgent a plan is, are written on separate notes.

sections.title: The SR Policy Association
sections.content:
Association type 6 is "SR Policy Association". Both peers must list type 6 in the ASSOC-Type-List TLV in their OPEN objects before using it. If both advertised the capability, the PCEP speaker that originates an SR Policy LSP MUST give it an SRPA. A missing SRPA draws a PCErr with Error-Type 6 and Error-value 22. An LSP may belong to at most one SRPA, since a candidate path cannot belong to several policies.

The SR Policy Identifier is the headend, color and endpoint. The Candidate Path Identifier is the protocol origin, originator and discriminator. Neither may change during the PCEP session, and no two candidate paths in a policy may share a candidate path identifier. Violations are answered with Error-Type 26 and Error-values 20 or 21. The optional attributes are the preference, the candidate path name and the policy name, and these MAY change.

The association parameters are fixed so that every speaker derives the same ones independently: the type is 6, the Association Source is the headend, the Association ID is always 1, and a mandatory Extended Association ID TLV (type 31) carries the color and endpoint. This avoids races when several speakers associate the same policy. A color-only policy uses an unspecified endpoint (0.0.0.0 or ::).
sections.plainLanguage: Every trip plan has a label made of who is starting, what kind of trip it is and where it ends. Each possible route also has its own tag. Once set, those tags are not changed.

sections.title: The SRPA TLVs
sections.content:
The SRPA object can carry four TLVs, and only the first instance of each type is processed.

  • SRPOLICY-POL-NAME (type 56, optional): the policy name, printable ASCII, with a recommended limit of 255 bytes.
  • SRPOLICY-CPATH-ID (type 57, mandatory, length 28): protocol origin, originator ASN, originator address and a 32-bit discriminator.
  • SRPOLICY-CPATH-NAME (type 58, optional): the candidate path name.
  • SRPOLICY-CPATH-PREFERENCE (type 59, optional, length 4): the preference, which defaults to 100 when the TLV is absent.

A missing mandatory TLV is answered with Error-Type 6 and Error-value 21. In a PCInitiate message the protocol origin is always 10, "PCEP". The TLVs are zero-padded to 4-octet alignment, and padding is not counted in the Length field.
sections.plainLanguage: The name tag has boxes to fill in. Some are required, like who made this route, and some are optional, like a nickname and how much you like it.

sections.title: Capabilities and LSP Object TLVs
sections.content:
Features that do not use the SRPA need their own capability exchange. The SRPOLICY-CAPABILITY TLV (type 71, length 4) goes in the OPEN object and carries four flags: P for computation priority, E for Explicit NULL Label policy, I for invalidation and L for stateless PCReq/PCRep operation. If a flag is 0, the peer MUST NOT send the matching TLV. Receiving an SRPA without this TLV having been exchanged draws Error-Type 10, Error-value 44, and the session is closed.

Three TLVs go in the LSP object. COMPUTATION-PRIORITY (type 68) holds an 8-bit priority for recomputation after a topology change; the lowest value is the highest priority and the default is 128. EXPLICIT-NULL-LABEL-POLICY (type 69) says whether an Explicit NULL label is pushed on unlabeled IP packets steered into the policy; it applies to SR-MPLS only and MUST be ignored for SRv6. INVALIDATION (type 70) controls Drop-Upon-Invalid.

With Drop-Upon-Invalid, an invalid LSP keeps attracting traffic and the headend drops it, instead of the traffic being redirected via the IGP or another LSP. The TLV carries an Oper byte and a Config byte, each with a D bit. The feature is enabled for the whole SR Policy, not one candidate path: if all candidate paths become invalid, the policy enters the drop state and activates the highest-preference candidate path that has it enabled.
sections.plainLanguage: Before chatting, each side says which extra tricks it knows. If a policy is broken, one trick says to throw packets away instead of sending them down some other road.

sections.title: Update to RFC 8231
sections.content:
RFC 8231 section 5.8.2 requires a PCReq before a PCRpt when delegating an LSP that is operationally down. This document makes that section not applicable to SR Policy LSPs, which are those set up with Path Setup Type 1 (SR) or 3 (SRv6). A PCC may go straight to sending PCRpt.

A speaker need not support PCReq/PCRep for SR Policies at all. It signals support with the L-flag, and when the flag is cleared or the capability TLV is absent, the peer MUST NOT send PCReq/PCRep for SR Policy LSPs. Other LSP types, such as RSVP-TE LSPs, are unaffected.
sections.plainLanguage: An old rule said you must ask before you tell. For these routes you can just tell, which saves messages.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
The SRPA object and TLVs could give an eavesdropper extra information about an SR Policy. The security considerations of RFC 5440, 8231, 8281, 8664, 8697, 9256 and 9603 apply. As in RFC 8231, these extensions are RECOMMENDED only on authenticated and encrypted sessions between PCEs and PCCs in the same administrative authority, using TLS as described in RFC 8253.

The manageability section follows RFC 6123 and covers configuration control, data models, liveness monitoring and impact on network operations.
sections.plainLanguage: The plans say where traffic goes, so keep the planner and routers talking over a locked line.

items.title: SR Policy Identifier
items.text: Headend, color and endpoint. Fixed for the session.

items.title: Candidate Path Identifier
items.text: Protocol origin, originator and discriminator. Fixed for the session.

items.title: Candidate Path attributes
items.text: Preference, candidate path name and policy name. May change.
